titleEn: Let my prayer stand as incense
progression: | Am Am | F F | C G | Am Am |
intro: Ten verses, an evening prayer, and the verse everyone knows is the second: let my prayer stand as incense before You, my lifted palms as the evening offering. What is unusual is what the speaker asks for first. Most psalms of this shape ask to be protected from enemies; this one asks to be protected from becoming one, with a guard posted on his own mouth and a request not to sit down at their table. Then verses 5 to 7 fall apart. They are among the hardest Hebrew in the book, the standard translations disagree with each other line by line, and the honest reading says so instead of smoothing them. Verses 8 to 10 come back to plain language and to the imagery of traps.

stichs.en: A psalm of David.
LORD, I have called You; hurry to me.
Listen to my voice when I call to You.

verses.summary: All urgency: four verbs of appeal in two short lines, with the calling stated at the start and repeated at the end so the verse closes where it opened.

stichs.en: Let my prayer stand as incense before You,
my lifted palms as the evening offering.

verses.summary: The request is not that the prayer be answered but that it be accepted, and the standard of acceptance is the evening service of the sanctuary.

stichs.en: Set a guard, LORD, over my mouth,
keep watch at the door of my lips.

verses.summary: A sentry posted on the speaker's own mouth. In the first half of this psalm the threat is what he might say, not what is said about him.

stichs.en: Do not let my heart lean toward an evil thing,
to busy myself with wicked deeds beside men who work iniquity,
and let me not taste their delicacies.

verses.summary: The longest verse, and the danger moves outward in stages: the heart leans, then the deeds are shared, then he is eating at their table. The last item is the smallest and the most concrete.

stichs.en: Let a righteous man strike me: that is kindness, and let him correct me.
Oil of the head, let my head not refuse it.
For still my prayer stands against their evils.

verses.summary: Here the Hebrew gets very hard. A blow from a righteous man is welcomed as kindness, and after that almost every word in the verse is contested.

stichs.en: Their judges were flung down by the hands of the rock,
and they heard my words, that they were sweet.

verses.summary: One of the most obscure verses in the book. Judges, a rock and sweet words are all there, and how the three connect is not recoverable with any confidence.

stichs.en: Like someone cleaving and splitting open the ground,
our bones are scattered at the mouth of Sheol.

verses.summary: Scattered bones at the mouth of Sheol, introduced by a comparison whose subject is never stated. The plural our arrives here without warning and does not return.

stichs.en: For my eyes are turned to You, LORD my Lord;
in You I have taken refuge, do not pour out my life.

verses.summary: The language clears. Eyes lifted, refuge taken, and one request: that the life not be tipped out the way water is emptied from a jar.

stichs.en: Keep me from the trap they have set for me,
and from the snares of those who work iniquity.

verses.summary: The imagery is hunting rather than warfare. The speaker is game, and what he asks for is not victory but simply not to be caught.

stichs.en: Let the wicked fall into his own nets, all of them together,
while I myself pass by.

verses.summary: The trap is turned around, and the closing word is not triumph but passage. He wants to get past, not to win.

pardes.body: The shape is clear even where the words are not. Verses 1 and 2 ask to be heard and set the standard for being heard, the evening service. Verses 3 and 4 ask for restraint, first on the mouth, then on the heart, then on the company kept and the food eaten with it. Verses 5 to 7 are the obscure centre. Verses 8 to 10 return to plain Hebrew and to hunting imagery: eyes lifted, refuge taken, traps, snares, nets. The unusual thing is the direction of the first request. Most psalms of this kind ask for protection from enemies; this one starts by asking for protection against joining them, and only reaches the enemies at the end.

Verses 5 to 7 are among the hardest Hebrew in the book, and the translations in circulation differ so widely that they cannot all be renderings of the same understood text. At {{5.4}} oil of the head can be choice oil or oil for anointing. The verb at {{5.7}} has no securely identified root and is often emended. At {{6.1}} the phrase reads by the hands of a rock, which is not idiomatic Hebrew for anything, and the subject, their judges, arrives after the verb. Verse 7 opens with a comparison whose subject is left unstated and ends with {{7.5}}, our bones, a first person plural found nowhere else in the psalm. Editors have proposed reconstructions and none has won agreement. The description that fits the evidence is that the text here may be damaged. What survives clearly is the vocabulary: kindness, rebuke, oil, prayer, judges, sweetness, bones, Sheol. The links between them do not.

Verse 2 is the verse the psalm is known by, and the reading that made it famous is that a prayer can occupy the slot an offering occupied. The incense of Exodus is burned in the morning and at dusk, and the daily offering has its second lamb toward evening, so the two halves of the verse point at the two evening acts of the sanctuary and pair them with two human ones, speech and lifted hands. Hosea makes the same move in chapter 14 with the words of the lips in place of bulls. Verse 3 has been taken in the other direction, not as substitution but as ethics: a guard is asked for the mouth in the same breath in which the mouth is offered, so the organ that prays is also the one that has to be watched. Read together the two verses make speech both the offering and the risk.

The choice of incense rather than a slaughtered animal carries the mystical reading. Incense leaves nothing behind, no meal and no hide, and the whole of it goes up as smoke, which makes it the offering that matches a prayer nobody hears. The lifted palms of {{2.5}} are the body copying that motion. Evening is associated in kabbalistic writing with judgement rather than with kindness, and an evening prayer therefore asks to be received rather than to be granted. That is why every request in this psalm is a restraint: guard the mouth, do not incline the heart, do not pour out the soul, keep me from the trap. Even the last verse asks only for passage, {{10.6}}, and not for a victory.
